en: *The Chapter on Repaying Kindness through Making Offerings to the Twelve Devas of Great Majestic Virtue*, one fascicle, translated by Amoghavajra.

At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, observing the humans and devas and feeling compassion for all, [proceeded] without interval... [self-... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment. The translation reflects the available portion.)
It is said that for all sentient beings, the four great elements undergo distant transformations,
resulting in various illnesses, or that ghosts and demons come to inflict various diseases.
The deluded world diminishes its lifespan.
How does one counteract such various internal and external harms?
It is because sentient beings do not recognize kindness.
Since there are such contradictions, on what basis can they be considered benefactors?
It is said that earth, water, fire, wind,
the sun, the moon, and the various devas all possess the grace of providing internal and external nourishment.
How can one repay such debts of gratitude?
This refers to the four great elements, as well as the essence of the heavens, the sun, the moon, and so forth.
Making offerings brings manifold benefits to the devas;
it causes both the vessel-world and the world of sentient beings to increase in strength.
For whom does this apply?
How many are there in number?
It is said that there are twelve such celestial realms:
the Earth Devas, Water Devas, Fire Devas, Wind Devas, Īśāna Devas, Śakra Devas, Yama Devas, Brahmā Devas, Vaiśravaṇa Devas, Rākṣasa Devas, Sun Devas, and Moon Devas.
When the Earth Deity is pleased, there are two benefits:
first, the human body becomes firm and its physical strength and vitality increase;
second, the flavor and potency of the earth element within the vessel-world (the environment) increase.
When these devas become angry, there are also two kinds of damage:
first, the bodies of human beings become disordered and ruined, and their physical complexion and strength diminish;
second, the vital essence of the earth within the physical world (bhājanaloka) all deviates from its original nature.
When Varuṇa is pleased, there are two benefits:
first, human beings do not suffer from thirst;
second, rain falls in accordance with the seasons.
When this deity becomes angry, there are likewise two kinds of harm:
first, human bodies become parched with thirst;
second, the vessel-world suffers from drought and pestilence until all things are completely dried up.
Alternatively, when it rains heavily and the world is filled with flowing water that might damage the grass but not reach the sentient beings,
there are two benefits at the time the Fire Deity rejoices:
first, the bodily heat of human beings increases or decreases according to the season.
Second, it does not oppose the seasons; furthermore, when this deity becomes angry, there are two types of harm:
first, the bodily heat of human beings increases or decreases at improper times;
second, natural fires spontaneously break out and incinerate all things.
When the wind deity rejoices, there are two benefits:
first, the human body experiences pliancy and its movements accord with the mind's intentions;
second, the physical world is peaceful and stable, free from upheaval or shaking.
Just as in the world there are cool winds that do not harm sentient or insentient beings when they are harmonious,
so too when this deity is angry, there are two kinds of harm:
first, the bodies and voices of human beings do not function according to their will.
Second, great winds blow, filling and shattering the world;
or there may be no wind at all, such that grasses and trees do not grow according to the seasons.
If such elemental essences exist, [the following occurs].
When the king and his people were afflicted by the wrath of the devas,
they entered the five-wheeled stūpa of the Tathāgata,
observed the various precepts, and took refuge in the Triple Gem.
Withdrawing the mind and abiding in stillness, one should contemplate in this way:
Earth arises dependent on water; because the nature of water is empty, earth is also impermanent.
Water arises dependent on wind; because the nature of wind is empty, water is also impermanent.
Fire depends on water and wind; because water and wind depend on space, fire is also impermanent.
Wind depends on empty space; because empty space has no substantial essence, wind is also impermanent.
Because wind is empty, fire is empty.
Because fire is empty, water is empty;
because water is empty, earth is empty;
because earth is empty, that which arises upon earth is empty.
When one contemplates that both sentient and insentient beings are entirely impermanent,
the anger of the devas is extinguished and they have no basis for abiding.
At that time, the practitioner again performs this contemplation:
although space is non-existent, there is still "space";
for this reason, it is given the name "space."
A name must necessarily have a corresponding entity. Because space exists, wind also exists;
because wind exists, fire, water, earth, and so forth all possess substantial entities.
When he contemplates in this way, the devas rejoice;
their majestic radiance increases manifold, and they abide in peace and security.
When Īśāna rejoices, the devas also rejoice.
The hosts of Māra do not cause disorder.
His former name was Maheśvara;
the Buddha said that if one makes offerings to Maheśvara—translated into Chinese as Dàzìzài (Great Sovereign)—one has already made offerings to all the devas.
When this deity becomes angry, the hosts of Māras all manifest the lands as desolate and in chaos.
Śakra, the Lord of Devas, is the ruler of those who dwell upon the earth;
he records the good and evil deeds committed by sentient beings.
When this deity is pleased, the land is peaceful and the people are not in turmoil;
when this deity is angry, there is conflict with weapons,
yet all the kings dwelling upon the earth remain secure.
When the deity Yama is pleased, people do not suffer untimely death and pestilence does not break out;
when this deity is angry, people die prematurely and pestilence fills the world.
As for Brahmā, he is the sovereign of the higher realms and the father of sentient beings.
At this time when the devas rejoice, the vessel-world (bhājanaloka) is peaceful and free from agitation. Why is this?
Because at the beginning of the kalpa...
This deity establishes the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
Sentient beings do not fall into disorder because he governs the world with justice. Why is this?
Because the Father King rejoices,
when this deity becomes angry,
the world is not at peace and various diseases arise.
As for the plants and trees, they all wither and fall;
sentient beings are deluded, like people who are intoxicated.
This is the time when Vaiśravaṇa rejoices.
The hosts of yakṣas rejoice in not harming the people;
they do not inflict poisonous swellings,
though they become utterly turbulent when provoked to anger.
When the rākṣasas rejoice,
all the flesh-eating spirits likewise rejoice;
they do not spit out poisonous vapors nor commit evil deeds.
When this deity is angry, all things appear in disorder;
when the Sun Deity is joyful, light does not diminish the objects.
When humans are angry, they become dull-witted, yet both sentient and insentient beings are entirely happy.
When this deva becomes angry, he loses his composure and his radiance;
though he possesses eyes, he cannot see objects,
and he is suddenly overcome by the suffering of cold.
When the Moon Deity is joyful, its cool light increases, and beings suffer no heat-related illnesses;
when it is angry, it withdraws them all.
When the sun and moon illuminate each other, there is great benefit, and the seasons are harmonious and balanced.
They rejoiced in every deed performed by sentient beings.
At the beginning of the kalpa, humans were like the gods of the Form Realm, but as they gradually craved flavors, their physical radiance diminished;
they abandoned virtuous minds and committed evil deeds.
The world is entirely non-compliant, experiencing both cold and heat;
therefore, these suns and moons, as celestial deities, manifest in the world as transformations and dreams.
Thus, these various deities are at times joyful and at times wrathful.
This refers to kings and their subjects who,
by failing to govern the world properly, commit unwholesome deeds;
they constantly practice killing and stealing, and abandon the True Dharma.
At that time, all the devas were filled with sorrow and anxiety;
their sorrow and anxiety having passed, they immediately gave rise to anger.
When celestial calamities were about to arise, there were first omens and portents.
This refers to rain falling without clouds.
When the stars appear in disorder and rain falls without clouds, this is the tears of the devas weeping; if they cease their evil karma, [the rain will stop].
When the world is governed with justice, the devas rejoice;
they all come to protect it, and a wondrous fragrance pervades everywhere.
Virtue increases and evil diminishes.
If a person understands that such great holy ones as the celestial beings adorn their birth-body with the gift of material wealth,
and subsequently manifest their dharma-body through the gift of the Dharma.
Furthermore, one should practice compassion and refrain from killing living beings;
this offering is made as a repayment for their kindness.
In the world, there are many devas and spirits, their number being exceedingly great.
Why is it that making offerings solely to these twelve devas establishes peace and happiness for the myriad people of the land?
It is because these twelve devas collectively encompass all devas, nāgas, spirits, ghosts, stars, and celestial officials.
Therefore, by making offerings and thoroughly understanding these twelve deities,
one immediately obtains the protection of all devas, nāgas, and so forth.
This is because the Earth Deity (Pṛthivī-devatā) and the various spirits upon the earth— including those dwelling beneath trees, in the wilderness, and as *piśāca* ghosts— [are thereby propitiated].
Varuṇa and all the deities of streams, rivers, great rivers, and the great ocean, together with the hosts of nāgas,
all came together into the maṇḍala to receive offerings simultaneously.
The Fire Deity, together with all the fire deities and the assembly of vidyādhara sages,
arrived at the maṇḍala and simultaneously received the offerings.
The Wind Deity, together with all the wind deities and the formless, wandering spirits, likewise arrived.
They all come together into the maṇḍala to receive offerings simultaneously.
Īśāna and his hosts of māras likewise come together into this maṇḍala to receive offerings simultaneously.
Śakra-devānām-indra, together with all the devas, ghosts, and others residing on Mount Sumeru and all other mountains,
came together to enter the maṇḍala and simultaneously receive offerings.
Yama-rāja, together with the officials of the five destinies, the Lord of Mount Tai, the deities of destiny, the plague-inflicting spirits, and various hungry ghosts, [likewise arrived].
They all came together into the maṇḍala to receive offerings simultaneously.
Brahmā and all the devas of the form realm who dwell in meditative concentration likewise came together into the maṇḍala to receive offerings simultaneously.

Vaiśravaṇa, together with the yakṣas, the devouring spirits, and the bhūtas, all came into the maṇḍala to receive offerings simultaneously; as did the rākṣasa devaputras and the hosts of blood-consuming rākṣasas.
They all come together to enter the maṇḍala and simultaneously receive offerings.
Sūrya, the Sun God, along with the host of stars, the seven luminaries, the various grahas, those who roam the sky, and all the deities of light,
all come together to enter the maṇḍala and simultaneously receive offerings.
The Moon Deity, together with all the twenty-eight lunar mansions dwelling in the sky, the twelve zodiac signs, and the entire host of constellations,
shall come together into the maṇḍala to receive offerings simultaneously;
one should contemplate it in this way.
Thus, in the presence of the Buddha,
the Lord of Devas personally vowed to bear the burden of all sentient beings, to protect the realms of nations, and to safeguard the True Dharma.
When invoked, he will never transgress his original vow and will certainly manifest his presence.
Until the time of dismissal,
those who abide in the ritual arena without violating their practice must first perform the invocation and offerings, and only then should they depart with gratitude.
Perform the various rites with relaxed ease and seek their favor.
At the time of invocation, one may use the individual mudrās and mantras for each deity,
or it is also permissible to use the general invocation mudrā and mantra.
How is it that a small amount of offered substance is enjoyed by various hosts of devas and spirits?
It is because a small offering, through three kinds of meanings, is enjoyed by all.
First, through the empowerment of the three secrets,
which is the sublime offering of the mind directed toward the true reality of the dharma-realm;
second, through great compassion.
Third, because the power of merit of those various celestial lords is great;
it is like a dragon that, having obtained a small amount of water, uses its own power of merit to sprinkle it throughout all kingdoms,
and by invoking the various heavens, fulfills the merit of the people of the four continents.
It does not equal the merit and wealth of even a single person among the gods of the Four Great Kings;
for while it increases or decreases according to the intentions of the presiding master who maintains it,
the merit of the various gods is vast.
One who receives meager offerings distributes them to all.
Just as a small fire increases or decreases according to the fuel,
so too it is with meager offerings.
Because his heavenly merit is abundant, it is entrusted to him to bring it to fulfillment and expansion.
Furthermore, even if its color and flavor are inferior,
by virtue of the three preceding meanings, it becomes entirely pure, subtle, and exquisite *amṛta* (clarified butter).
Just as when Jīvaka takes pity on all beings, all things become medicine;
or as when a Nigaṇṭha recites incantations over poison, the poison itself turns back into medicine—
so it is even in the world.
How much more so for a practitioner who follows the Buddha’s teachings,
giving rise to great compassion and performing the empowerment of the three secrets!
Furthermore, by virtue of celestial merit, even those inferior offerings [become sublime].
They accomplished pure and sublime offerings, like a man who grinds stone to become a king,
or a worldly woman who takes sand and makes it gold;
the assembly of Queen Śyāmā did not indulge in worldly wealth, but took sole delight in following what is correct.
For this reason, one does not slight even small offerings, but delights in the compassionate giving of gifts.
If the deity is not pleased, one should instead request the four-armed Acala, the wrathful vidyārāja and lord of the external Vajra Family, for worship and refuge.
At that time, the various devas, complying with the instructions, joyfully protected and sustained [the ritual].
When making offerings, where do they take their positions?
It is said: Śakra is in the east, and Agni is in the southeast.
In the south is Yama; in the southwest, the rākṣasas;
in the west, Varuṇa; in the northwest, Vāyu;
in the north, Vaiśravaṇa; and in the northeast, Īśāna.
The central principal deity is flanked by Brahmā, the Earth Deity, the Sun Deity, and the Moon Deity at the four corners;
they abide in this manner.
How should one make offerings, and which deity should be regarded as the foremost?
That is to say, one may offer according to the cardinal directions, beginning from the east and proceeding clockwise; or,
having a specific aspiration, one may make offerings according to rites such as those for pacifying calamities (*śāntika*).
If seeking pacification, Śakra is the principal deity;
if seeking increase, Brahmā is the presiding deity;
if seeking subjugation, Maheśvara is the principal deity.
If one seeks respect and affection, Vaiśravaṇa is the principal deity,
while the others are offered as subordinate attendants;
if one desires to pacify weapons and warfare, Śakra is the principal deity.
If one wishes to eliminate the calamities of yakṣas and rākṣasas, one should employ Vaiśravaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasa devas.
If one wishes to eliminate pestilence, one should employ Yama.
If one wishes to eliminate the calamities of drought-demons and floods, one employs Varuṇa, the water deity, in both cases.
If one wishes to eliminate enmity and calamities, one should employ Vāyu-deva;
furthermore, one may pray to this deity for protection against wind-related disasters and the like.
If one wishes to harmonize people, one should employ Brahmā-deva.
For water-related calamities, employ the deity Agni;
for fire-related calamities, employ the deity Varuṇa;
for subduing Māra, employ the deity Īśāna.
Alternatively, one may employ Agni (the Fire Deity) to suppress malevolent locations and Prthivī (the Earth Deity) to pray for the five grains.
If one seeks official rank, one should employ Śakra-devendra;
if one seeks wisdom, one should employ Sūrya; if one seeks meditative concentration, one should employ Candra.

If one wishes to eliminate the afflictions of heat or cold, one should employ either Sūrya or Candra accordingly: Sūrya removes cold, while Candra removes heat. If there are diseases of the four great elements, [one should likewise employ them].
According to their respective functions, the deities of the four great elements are the foremost;
the others are to be honored in succession according to their order.
For the sake of wealth, he used Vaiśravaṇa;
for the sake of nobility, he further used Brahmā.
For each of these offerings, he prepared a vessel.
One should place incense, unguents, seasonal flowers, the five grains, cooked rice, or gruel, as well as wax candles and other such items,
in a single vessel and offer them; one should burn incense so that it pervades everywhere,
making the offering pure and in accordance with the Dharma.
The specific mudrās and mantras for each offering ritual,
as well as the various doctrinal meanings concerning the painted images, are as explained in other sections.
Thus, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, in order to deliver sentient beings, [taught these].
One asks oneself and answers oneself regarding such causes and conditions,
such requitals of gratitude, such prayers,
such contemplations of the Dharma, and such three secrets.
With such skillful means and such great power,
he expounded this at will and presented it to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One declared that the meaning and principle were indeed thus.
Excellent, excellent! What you have said is true and not false.
These twelve devas are indeed former Buddhas who have appeared in this world to deliver sentient beings.
Therefore, a practitioner must not rely on the celestial realms of physical form;
rather, they should contemplate the adornments of the Dharma-body of those heavens.
If a person follows what I and you have said, [they will attain this].
The devas are worthy of offerings.
By reciting and studying the profound Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā sutras before these images of the devas,
one causes all these devas to experience great joy.
Because the devas rejoice,
all sentient beings attain joy; those who attain it, all sentient beings rejoice.
Therefore, all Buddhas also rejoice.
Because all Buddhas rejoice,
the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of both the mundane and supramundane realms are perfected.
One fascicle of the Ritual Manual for the Twelve Deva Kings.
